story.headline: Attacks on ships and Saudi refineries in the Gulf pulled gold and oil back up this week, ending their November slides. The loonie gained most and the yen least, with a December Fed hike near certain.

reads.policy: A December Fed hike is all but certain, which keeps the dollar firm. The European Central Bank, Bank of England, Bank of Japan and Bank of Canada are all still expected to hike in December, though soft French and Spanish inflation weakens the case for more European hikes after that.
reads.growth: Chinese factory profits grew strongly, good news for Australia. The US goods trade gap widened sharply as imports of artificial intelligence equipment surged, a drag on US growth this quarter. Germany's labour market softened, and Canada's growth figures on Monday are expected to show a sharp slowdown.
reads.inflation: Inflation cooled far more than expected in France and Spain as fuel got cheaper, which weighed on the euro. US and Australian inflation still run hot, keeping their central banks leaning toward higher rates.
reads.risk: A slide in technology shares midweek briefly sent money into the yen and franc, then stocks recovered. Gulf attacks on ships kept worry high, and that worry went into gold rather than currencies.
reads.tot: Oil rose on the week for the first time in four weeks, which helped the Canadian dollar most. Gold's rebound gives the Aussie a lift. OPEC+'s decision on Sunday sets the tone for both.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Heavy bets against the loonie leave room for a fast unwind if Canadian hike bets keep growing.
reads.fiscal: S&P kept France's credit rating but cut its outlook to negative, so all three big agencies now see a possible downgrade, a weight on the euro. New Zealand's government is one seat short of a majority, which adds doubt over its spending.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. Traders fully expect a quarter-point hike on December 9.
fed.priced: December: quarter-point hike all but certain. January: another hike a little more likely than not.
fed.why: US growth was revised up to a 4.3% pace and core inflation rose to 3.3%, well above the Fed's 2% goal. US bond yields rose again on Friday, November 27, a sign markets still see more hikes ahead.
fed.watch: The November jobs report on Friday, December 4, the last big data before the decision on December 9, which comes with new forecasts from officials.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October. Governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday, November 24 the bank may need to act sooner, and all six of Canada's biggest banks now expect a December hike.
boc.why: Governor Tiff Macklem warned the oil shock will keep prices sticky and said the bank was too slow to spot lasting inflation after the pandemic. Oil still near $95 a barrel adds to that worry.
boc.watch: Canada's third-quarter growth on Monday, November 30, the jobs report on Friday, December 4, and oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the final election count left the government needing a new partner.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures and stronger spending argue for a hike, while unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: Coalition talks after the final election count left the government one seat short, and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October, and the record of that meeting showed many officials were ready to hike then. A December hike is widely expected, and euro-area leaders picked Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed President Christine Lagarde in February 2027.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, and Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel warned it could stay above 3% into 2027. Cooling prices in France and Spain, slow German growth and France's debts argue for stopping after December.
ecb.watch: Germany's November inflation on Monday, November 30 and the euro area's on Tuesday, December 1, after France and Spain came in soft. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Tokyo's inflation reached a 16-month high in November, though mainly because of energy.
boj.why: Costly energy, a weak yen and strong demand are pushing prices up, and board member Naoki Tamura has floated a bigger hike. But prices outside food and energy cooled in Tokyo, which argues for a steady pace.
boj.watch: Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech on Monday, November 30, and any sign Japan steps in to support the yen near 160 to the dollar. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Inflation jumped to 4.9% in October and business investment surged, which ended bets on a cut soon.
rba.priced: December: hold expected. Cuts in 2027 now look less likely.
rba.why: Inflation is well above the bank's 2–3% target and firms are still spending hard. The International Monetary Fund has backed the bank's leaning toward higher rates, though job losses argue for a pause in December.
rba.watch: Australia's third-quarter growth on the evening of Tuesday, December 1 CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, and markets lean toward another hike on December 17. Its Financial Stability Report on Thursday, November 26 gave no new signal on rates.
boe.why: Governor Andrew Bailey said inflation may peak lower if energy prices hold, while policymaker Catherine Mann wants more hikes sooner. High fuel costs still keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal.
boe.watch: Any comments from officials, after Governor Andrew Bailey and two colleagues sounded split before lawmakers on Wednesday, November 25. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Falls in stock markets or Gulf clashes that send money into the franc, and the new US tariff plans for Swiss goods. The decision is December 10.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits at the top of the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Hot inflation and strong business investment make cuts unlikely, and calmer stock markets lifted it off its lowest this year.

GBP.summary: The pound sits second on the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight, and markets lean toward another Bank of England hike in December. It still trades near a one-year low against the dollar.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High US interest rates and a fast-growing economy support it, while large budget deficits weigh. A December Fed hike is fully expected, and the dollar trades near its highest in almost two years.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm dairy prices help, but doubts over a December rate hike and an election that left the government one seat short keep it near its lowest since 2009.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Germany's economy is barely growing, inflation is cooling in France and Spain, and S&P has turned negative on France's debts. It ended the week near $1.094, not far above its weakest in about 19 months.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board, because recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. Firm oil and a widely expected December Bank of Canada hike made it the strongest of the eight this week.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A likely December Bank of Japan hike and the threat of Japan stepping in keep the dollar just under 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. It gains when fear sends money its way, and gives that back when markets calm.
